newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia threatens to outlaw truckers' strike.
newsitem.headline: Colombia threatens to outlaw truckers' strike.

text.p: Colombian truck drivers entered the fourth day of a crippling nationwide strike on Thursday after talks aimed at hammering out a peaceful settlement ended in what union officials described as total deadlock.

Transporation Minister Carlos Hernan Lopez held more than seven hours of talks late on Wednesday with the Colombian Truck Drivers Association in a bid to put an end to the strike that has clamped a virtual stranglehold on the economy.

But Alvaro Santacruz, a union official and one of the participants in the talks, said very little headway was made. He said Lopez had threatened to declare the strike illegal unless the association agreed to end the action, which has halted all shipments of coffee and other key commodities to Colombia's ports.

It was not immediately clear what the government would achieve by outlawing the strike and Santacruz said drivers were determined to continue pressing their demands, the most important of which is a call for higher shipping rates.
Higher rates would translate into better wages for truckers, Santacruz said, adding "we're not looking to get rich but we're entitled to make a decent living."

Lopez, arguing that the government's hands are tied, has insisted shipping rates are set by individual transportation companies and the laws of supply and demand, not by state regulators. But the Drivers Association wants the government intercede on its behalf with representatives of the transportation companies.

Santacruz said talks with Lopez and other Transportation Ministry officials were set to resume on Thursday afternoon. But he said only about five percent of truckers' demands had been resolved in Wednesday's round of talks, and the negotiating process promised to be a long one.
With virtually all deliveries to Colombia's ports suspended since the strike began at midnight Sunday, exporters say coffee promises to be one of the hardest hit industries.

"We're missing the steamers already," one leading private coffee exporter said on Thursday. He estimated that at least 250,000 132-pound (60-kilo) bags of coffee of the 630,000 bags that private exporters had committed for delivery in October would not reach the market until November.

The prices of fresh produce and basic foodstuffs in major cities have skyrocketed because of shortages caused by the strike and what the Agriculture Ministry described in a communique late on Wednesday as price gouging by store owners.
Pumping operations along Colombia's two main oil pipelines resumed on Thursday after a 24-hour paralysis caused by a separate oil workers' union's strike, the state oil company Ecopetrol said.

The union ordered the stoppage to pressure the government to restructure Ecopetrol, which it fears may be a step away from eventual privatisation, and to protest demands by British Petroleum to renegotiate an association contract with Ecopetrol.
